sections.heading: Lead
Inspiration and writing
sections.wikitext:
When Bee Gees manager [[Robert Stigwood]] was producing a movie about a New York [[disco]] scene, the working title for the film at that time was ''Saturday Night''. Stigwood asked the group to write a song using that name as a title, but the Bee Gees disliked it. They had already written a song called "Night Fever", so the group convinced Stigwood to use that and change the film to ''Saturday Night Fever''.<ref name="disco">{{cite web|url=http://www.songfacts.com/detail.php?id=5534 |title=Night Fever by Bee Gees |publisher=Songfacts.com |access-date=12 February 2015}}</ref>

The string intro of "Night Fever" was inspired by "[[Theme from A Summer Place|Theme from ''A Summer Place'']]" by [[Percy Faith]], according to keyboardist [[Blue Weaver]].<ref name="disco"/> As Weaver explains the history behind this song:

{{quote|...'Night Fever' started off because Barry walked in one morning when I was trying to work out something. I always wanted to do a disco version of Theme from ''A Summer Place'' by the Percy Faith Orchestra or something - it was a big hit in the Sixties. I was playing that, and Barry said, 'What was that?' and I said, 'Theme from ''A Summer Place''', and Barry said, 'No, it wasn't'. It was new. Barry heard the idea - I was playing it on a string [[synthesizer]] and sang the riff over it.<ref name="riff">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Uzv_AgAAQBAJ&q=too+much+heaven+bee+gees&pg=PT764 |title=The Bee Gees |author1=Melinda Bilyeu |author2=Hector Cook |author3=Andrew Môn Hughes |date=January 2011 |publisher=Omnibus Press |isbn=9780857128942 |access-date=14 February 2015}}</ref>|Blue Weaver}}

Barry Gibb, [[Robin Gibb]] and [[Maurice Gibb]] completed the lyrics for "Night Fever" sitting on a staircase (reminiscent of their first international hit "[[New York Mining Disaster 1941]]", which was also written in a staircase back in 1967).<ref name="riff"/>
sections.text:
When Bee Gees manager Robert Stigwood was producing a movie about a New York disco scene, the working title for the film at that time was Saturday Night. Stigwood asked the group to write a song using that name as a title, but the Bee Gees disliked it. They had already written a song called "Night Fever", so the group convinced Stigwood to use that and change the film to Saturday Night Fever.

The string intro of "Night Fever" was inspired by "Theme from A Summer Place" by Percy Faith, according to keyboardist Blue Weaver. As Weaver explains the history behind this song:

{{quote|...'Night Fever' started off because Barry walked in one morning when I was trying to work out something. I always wanted to do a disco version of Theme from A Summer Place by the Percy Faith Orchestra or something - it was a big hit in the Sixties. I was playing that, and Barry said, 'What was that?' and I said, 'Theme from A Summer Place, and Barry said, 'No, it wasn't'. It was new. Barry heard the idea - I was playing it on a string synthesizer and sang the riff over it.|Blue Weaver}}

Barry Gibb, Robin Gibb and Maurice Gibb completed the lyrics for "Night Fever" sitting on a staircase (reminiscent of their first international hit "New York Mining Disaster 1941", which was also written in a staircase back in 1967).

sections.heading: Recording
sections.wikitext:
The Bee Gees began recording the song by April 1977 in France and finished it in September the same year. A demo of "Night Fever" with some instrumental and vocals heard on it exists and was available to download on [[Rhino Records]]' website in 2009 or earlier.<ref name="criteria"/>

{{quote|...For 'Night Fever' the group had the hook-line and rhythm - they usually pat their legs to set up a song's rhythm when they first sing it - and parts of the verses. They had the emotion, same as on the record. We put down [[Drum kit|battery]] first, so the feel was locked in. The [[electric piano]] part was put on before the bass, then the heavy guitar parts. We had the sound, but we needed something there to shake it so we used the thunder sound.<ref name="riff"/>|[[Albhy Galuten]]}}

sections.heading: Reception
sections.wikitext:
According to ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', it has a "jumping disco beat" and a "smooth falsetto lead" vocal.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Billboard|title=Hot Single Picks|access-date=2020-07-10|page=88|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-Billboard/70s/1978/Billboard%201978-02-04.pdf|date=4 February 1978}}</ref> ''[[Cash Box]]'' similarly said that it has "dancin' beat, scratchy guitar, sweeping orchestration and the familiar falsetto."<ref name=cb>{{cite news|title=CashBox Singles Reviews|date=February 4, 1978|page=18|newspaper=Cash Box|access-date=2021-12-26|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/70s/1978/CB-1978-02-04.pdf}}</ref> ''[[Record World]]'' predicted that it would become "another dance tempo hit" for the Bee Gees.<ref name=rw>{{cite magazine|magazine=Record World|date=February 4, 1978|access-date=2023-02-15|title=Hits of the Week|page=1|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Record-World/70s/78/RW-1978-02-04.pdf}}</ref>

According to  [[Allmusic]] critic Donald A. Guarisco, the lyrics "a disco fan looking for love on the dancefloor" and the song "convincingly recreates the euphoria disco fans feel while dancing to their beloved music" with lyrics such as "Here I am prayin' for this moment to last/Livin' on the music, so fine."<ref name=allmusic>{{cite web|title=Night Fever|author=Guarisco, Donald A.|publisher=Allmusic|accessdate=2026-02-09|url=https://www.allmusic.com/song/night-fever-mt0045196992}}</ref> Guarisco praised the song's [[hook (music)|hook]]s, rhythm. string arrangement and [[falsetto]] harmonies, concluding that the "combination of hip lyrics and an infectious melody truly capture the appeal of disco.".<ref name=allmusic/>
sections.text:
According to Billboard, it has a "jumping disco beat" and a "smooth falsetto lead" vocal. Cash Box similarly said that it has "dancin' beat, scratchy guitar, sweeping orchestration and the familiar falsetto." Record World predicted that it would become "another dance tempo hit" for the Bee Gees.

According to  Allmusic critic Donald A. Guarisco, the lyrics "a disco fan looking for love on the dancefloor" and the song "convincingly recreates the euphoria disco fans feel while dancing to their beloved music" with lyrics such as "Here I am prayin' for this moment to last/Livin' on the music, so fine." Guarisco praised the song's hooks, rhythm. string arrangement and falsetto harmonies, concluding that the "combination of hip lyrics and an infectious melody truly capture the appeal of disco.".

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.wikitext:
The song replaced [[Andy Gibb]]'s "[[(Love Is) Thicker Than Water|Love Is Thicker Than Water]]" at number one and was in turn replaced by [[Yvonne Elliman]]'s "[[If I Can't Have You (Bee Gees song)|If I Can't Have You]]"—all of which were written and produced by the Gibb brothers. It would be the third of six consecutive US number-ones for the band, tying [[the Beatles]] for the record for most consecutive number-one singles. ''Billboard'' ranked it as the No. 2 song for 1978, behind Andy Gibb's "[[Shadow Dancing (song)|Shadow Dancing]]".<ref>[[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1978]]</ref>

"Night Fever" topped the [[UK Singles Chart]] for two weeks, their third UK number-one, and in the US it remained the number-one [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] single for over two months in 1978. In addition to ''Saturday Night Fever'', the song appeared in the movie and on the soundtrack for ''[[Mystery Men]]''. The song is listed at number 38 on ''Billboard's All Time Top 100''.<ref name="Bronson 6">{{cite magazine|url= http://www.billboard.com/articles/list/2155531/the-hot-100-all-time-top-songs?list_page=6 |title= Hot 100 55th Anniversary: The All-Time Top 100 Songs |magazine= Billboard|date= 2 August 2012 |access-date= 9 August 2013 |first= Fred |last= Bronson}}</ref> It is also featured in other films including ''[[La Luna (1979 film)|Luna]]'', ''[[Mr. Saturday Night]]'', ''[[I.D. (1995 film)|I.D.]]'', ''[[Whatever Happened to Harold Smith?]]'' and ''[[Avenue Montaigne (film)|Avenue Montaigne]]''.
sections.text:
The song replaced Andy Gibb's "Love Is Thicker Than Water" at number one and was in turn replaced by Yvonne Elliman's "If I Can't Have You"—all of which were written and produced by the Gibb brothers. It would be the third of six consecutive US number-ones for the band, tying the Beatles for the record for most consecutive number-one singles. Billboard ranked it as the No. 2 song for 1978, behind Andy Gibb's "Shadow Dancing".

"Night Fever" topped the UK Singles Chart for two weeks, their third UK number-one, and in the US it remained the number-one Billboard Hot 100 single for over two months in 1978. In addition to Saturday Night Fever, the song appeared in the movie and on the soundtrack for Mystery Men. The song is listed at number 38 on Billboard's All Time Top 100. It is also featured in other films including Luna, Mr. Saturday Night, I.D., Whatever Happened to Harold Smith? and Avenue Montaigne.

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext: A music video was made for the song in 1978 but not shown to the public until 26 years later, in 2004.{{citation needed|date=May 2012}} It features the brothers singing the song in a darkened studio, layered over background video filmed while driving along "Motel Row" on Collins Avenue, a {{convert|3|mi|adj=on|0}} motel strip in what is now [[Sunny Isles Beach, Florida]].<ref>{{YouTube|-ihs-vT9T3Q|"Bee Gees - Night Fever (Video)"}}. Retrieved on 2020-10-27.</ref> Most of the motels which appear in the video are now closed or demolished, including several whose names are reminiscent of Las Vegas resorts (Castaways, Desert Inn, Sahara, Golden Nugget).{{citation needed|date=July 2020}}

In 1996, the Austrian music group Ex-It covered the song and made a small notable success. Large parts of the original were retained in this version, but with many rap passages added. This cover is the compilations ''Dance Now! 14'', ''Maxi Dance Sensation 21'' and ''Hot Hits [TL 541/35]''.

In 1996, the Austrian music group Ex-It covered the song and made a small notable success. Large parts of the original were retained in this version, but with many rap passages added. This cover is the compilations Dance Now! 14, Maxi Dance Sensation 21 and Hot Hits [TL 541/35].

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext: The music video copies many elements of the movie ''[[Saturday Night Fever]]'' and satirizes the same. At the beginning of the video, the DJ plays the song, while the protagonist and his girlfriend in a tool shop look around and watch a radio. They then prepare for a visit to a disco and are seen dancing throughout the rest of the video.
